title: The People Who Feed Us Are on Their Own — TikTok
notes: Hook question: the people who grow America's food work constantly, so why are they about to lose their health coverage? Answer, scene by scene: rural jobs rarely come with insurance, so farmers lean on the ACA and Medicaid; the ACA subsidies just expired; Medicaid work rules start Jan 1 and cut people over paperwork, not work; the unemployment exemption barely covers any counties. The close: those who feed the country shouldn't do it alone.
All figures are from the article (Nov 18, 2026) and the sources it cites (KFF, ACS 2024, CBO, NEJM, Nebraska Hospital Association, BLS). Co-authored post, so the narration uses 'we'.
VOICE: ElevenLabs, generated only after the author approves the script. Render drafts with the default --voice keep.

post.headline: The people who feed us are losing coverage
post.caption: Farmers buy their own health insurance at 3 times the rate of other adults, and their premiums just jumped when ACA subsidies expired. On January 1, Medicaid work rules start, and in Arkansas 92% of people who lost coverage had actually met the rules.
post.cta: Full story and interactive maps at the link in bio.

say: Meghan and John Palmer milk 180 cows in Iowa.

scenes.source: The People Who Feed Us Are on Their Own · American Inequality
say: When the ACA subsidies expired this year, their monthly health bill jumped more than 90%, with a $7,200 deductible on top.
We looked at why the people who grow America's food are about to lose even more coverage.
It starts with jobs. In rural counties, fewer workers get insurance through work, so far more rely on public programs.

scenes.title: Share who buy coverage on the ACA marketplace
say: 27% of farmers and ranchers buy their own coverage on the ACA marketplace, about 3 times the rate of other adults.

overlays.label: of U.S. food is grown by American farmers

scenes.source: The People Who Feed Us Are on Their Own · American Inequality
say: These are the people who grow 85% of America's food, and seasonal workers do 60% of the crop labor.
In rural places like eastern Kentucky, more than half of residents rely on Medicaid.

overlays.text: 80 HOURS A MONTH, PROVEN ON PAPER

say: Starting January 1, Medicaid adults must prove 80 hours a month of work, school or service to keep their coverage.

scenes.title: Arkansas, 2018: people who lost Medicaid under work rules

bars.label: Had met the rules or should have been exempt

say: When Arkansas tried this in 2018, 18,000 people lost coverage, and 92% of them had met the rules or should have been exempt.
In Nebraska, which started early, Eli McCreary lost coverage in the middle of kidney cancer treatment.
States can exempt counties with high unemployment, but only 144 counties qualify, since the rural problem is low-wage and seasonal work, not joblessness.

overlays.label: people projected to lose Medicaid by 2034

say: By 2034, more than five million people are projected to lose Medicaid because of the paperwork and deadlines.
Congress has promised to reverse the cuts, but the work rules start two days before the new members are even sworn in.

scenes.text: Those who feed the country {shouldn't do it alone.}
say: The Palmers will keep milking cows and picking up nursing shifts, but those who feed the country should not have to do it alone.
You can read the full story on American Inequality.
